• Qualcomm litigation (Round 2) outcome (late 2026), and
• Licensee strategy shifts that reduce Arm dependency
Absent these headwinds, we see scope for a material re-rating.
Where could we be wrong? We see 3 key upside risks to our thesis:
• Faster than expected adoption of agentic systems could accelerate chip deployment and drive earlier upside.
• Further product announcements over the next 2–3 years may mitigate execution and competitive concerns.
• Improved disclosure around underlying licensing growth could alleviate investor concerns regarding revenue concentration.

Idea
Executive Summary
An Agentic Arm. Arm's new design is a change in business model that could transform the topline but also change the margin profile. In short, we think Arm’s chip initiative is well timed and strategically coherent. While the long-term case remains compelling, the transition carries execution, competitive, and cyclical risks. We see limited scope for near-term multiple expansion, but remain constructive on the medium- to long-term opportunity.
Below we outline the transition to chipmaking brought by the rollout of agentic AI and show why the CPU is not 'dead' in AI. Elsewhere, we discuss the growing cores per GW, look at the relevance to agentic workflows and appreciate that more could follow. But there are also concerns around potential for a customer backlash. How Arm balances this multi-year transition is a debate.
A new chip
Arm has created a dual-chiplet CPU with class-leading performance per watt. There has been a lot of customer engagement, it dovetails new agentic drivers well, and it trades on power efficiency and lower total cost of ownership (TCO) relative to x86 (Intel, AMD). It is positioned for winning share relative to x86 in agentic workflows, which is likely a key driver for future sales growth. And yet, sales will be small for now. We think it likely this business will be loss making for a while (we estimate until 2029, given initial high opex), but Arm has solid growth targets for 5 years out, which the company said are based on line of sight with key customers (Meta, OpenAI, etc.). Other customers, such as SAP, Cloudflare, F5 and Cerebras, are also involved, and we expect Arm's pricing to be competitive. All told, this is a solid debut for Arm in fabless chipmaking.
Morgan Stanley Research

Morgan Stanley RESEARCH Why now? The Arm AGI CPU is a 3nm, TSMC fabbed chip initially built with lead partner Meta but will be shippable to other customers, such as OpenAI and Cerebras, in time. We view this transition as timely, given the development of agentic inference and what it means for CPU provision in AI. As new agentic frameworks, such as OpenClaw, gain in popularity, we expect a resulting rise in agentic workflows. These drive a new fabric layer that seeks to manage the functioning of the agentic system by using new CPU designs. Some hyperscalers are more exposed to this than others – arguably that includes META (covered by Brian Nowak) and OpenAI. This is driven by the need for enhanced orchestration for agents, as well as partly by a growing number of cores per chip over this period. Their expectation may also reflect a likely rollout of new high performance, high efficiency cores and even a change in ratio of CPU:GPU that could flip from the common 1:2 to something closer to 2:1 or even 4:1 in time, given their growing importance in agentic workflows. The idea that the CPU is irrelevant in AI cloud has been scotched, thanks to the rollout of agentic inference. Peer Comparison The Arm AGI CPU can be thought of as a mid-market chip, different to Nvidia's Vera, which was clearly designed with the Nvidia system in mind. This gives the chip the broadest market appeal. The AGI chip focuses on power efficiency, a single-threaded compute, as well as a performance design to handle most agentic tasks and scalability. Milestones to our bull case
Pending full execution, we see material upside to our bull case. Assuming zero risk to our 5-year forecasts and discounting back to today values Arm shares at $287, or up c.79% from here.
And yet to see this re-rate, Arm would need to traverse three sentiment hurdles, in our view:
(i) The impact of DRAM shortages on client royalties (timing: Q1/Q2 reporting season). The rising price of DRAM contracts is one obstacle, but the availability of memory is becoming scarce for handsets, laptops and other consumer electronic devices. We expect the resulting allocation of DRAM supply to impact some handset availability, especially Android-based handsets (see our Global Insight note here). Arm is not overly exposed in $- terms, given the relative v9/CSS (higher $-rates) incident in premium smartphones, which are likely to remain less affected, and yet the uncertainty may weigh on royalty assumptions into FY27e. We look to the next two reporting seasons to bring more clarity here. Beyond this we expect the market to renew focus on Arm's own chip developments.
(ii) 'Round 2' litigation with Qualcomm creates overhang (timing; late 2026). Last year's litigation proceedings with Qualcomm (link) resulted in a setback ruling for Arm. The court found largely in Qualcomm's favour, suggesting Arm's ability to charge higher royalty rates in architectural license agreements may be limited, at least in Qualcomm's case. Following the previous trial, Qualcomm filed a separate lawsuit against Arm in January 2025. This upcoming 2026 case (often referred to as 'Round 2') centres on

Once the litigation overhang has ultimately been cleared, we would expect investor sentiment to improve as focus returns to Arm's strategic move into chips. Qualcomm is covered by Joseph Moore.
(iii) Investor concerns that licensees may shift reliance off Arm IP. Arm's shift into chip making raises questions of competition with existing licensee partners. In particular, investors have raised concerns on whether potential customer unease over competition could lead to eventual Arm independence; however, management highlighted that the CPU market is unfulfilled and is large enough for multiple players to coexist. Large, well covered partners like Nvidia and Apple (the latter covered by Erik Woodring) already have long term licensing agreements and likely have all the Arm access they need. They are unlikely to change behaviour meaningfully, in our view. Others may be less covered. Although Arm licenses its Neoverse V3 CPU cores, it is unlikely to license the full AGI CPU design as IP – that’s not the business model. This means Arm might end up competing with some customers in the cloud CPU space. Such licensees could conceivably seek to de-emphasise reliance on Arm. But such a move would not likely be easy (premium alternatives don't exist) and would imply a slow, multi-year initiative involving a fair degree of business risk to these licensees and perhaps to Arm sentiment. We make no changes to our licensing and royalties forecasts, given this degree of risk, but highlight this as a potential sentiment overhang all the same.
Financials & Valuation
How have we forecast this opportunity?
Arm's stated TAM is perhaps conservative but seems to assume c.30% market share for ARM in their SAM (c.$50bn).
We make several modelling assumptions including:
• The amount of MW adds over the next five years by key customers, looking at GW class projects in particular and making assumptions of enterprise take up.
• An annual roadmap of new generations of CPU design, ranging from 136 cores today to 500+ by Gen5 for 2030+.
• Pricing that starts at $2k+ but also includes some discounting for key development partner Meta
• Margins that, as management say, start at c.40% (given reliance on back-end silicon vendor support) and climb eventually to 50%+ on higher ASPs and greater use of in-house capabilities (including closer collaboration with other SoftBank affiliates, such as Ampere).
Our previous model didn’t include working capital estimates, as Arm was a standalone IP business. With the introduction of the chip business, we estimate 60 payable days, 40 receivable days and 90 inventory days. This is broadly in-line with the working capital trend of fabless chipmaker peers. We expect the payable days and inventory days to trend down as the chip business becomes more established and the company works towards a net positive working capital.

How We Got Here
Shifting to Agentic AI Systems
Agentic AI represents the next stage in AI evolution, enabling machines to act more like autonomous agents, rather than passive tools. Unlike with Generative AI ('GenAI'), which predicts the next token, Agentic AI is about autonomy – making decisions, taking actions, and driving outcomes with minimal human oversight.
Agentic AI represents a fundamental advance in AI. New advancements in AI modelling technology (reasoning, reinforcement learning), together with new protocols (e.g., MCP), are making this AI evolution possible. Unlike with earlier AI systems that provided oneshot responses, Agentic AI can reason step-by-step, breaking down problems methodically. This reasoning capability requires significantly more compute resources.
Deeper Architectural Shift. The broader shift is a transition from model-centric to workflow-centric systems. Previously, products were defined by a single model call, with intelligence concentrated inside the model itself. Increasingly, we expect AI cloud products will be defined by orchestrated workflows made up of multiple models and tools, with intelligence distributed across the fabric layer. In this way, agentic workflows become the user-facing interface, while inference–fabric separation becomes the underlying infrastructure.
Agentic Workflows
Our core argument is that the rise of agentic workflows is driving a structural separation in compute – a disaggregation between the inference layer and the fabric layer. The relationship is bi-directional – agentic workflows necessitate this separation, and separation in turn enables agentic systems to scale effectively and operate with greater control.

Morgan Stanley RESEARCH
Idea
• Agentic workflows are multi-step, goal-directed systems in which AI agents plan actions, invoke tools or APIs, and iterate on intermediate results.
• Agents may also collaborate with one another, forming multi-agent systems.
• As these workflows proliferate, AI usage is shifting away from single, user-initiated model prompts toward automated orchestration, reasoning loops, and continuous execution (always-on).
Note: The fabric layer can dynamically route tasks to different models based on complexity and cost, maintain persistent memory and state across long time horizons, and integrate with external APIs, databases, and enterprise systems. It also enables observability, governance, and policy enforcement, capabilities that are critical for production and enterprise deployment.
Inference-Fabric Separation
Inference–fabric separation reflects a change in AI system design. Model execution (at the inference layer) is being disaggregated from orchestration & control functions (in the fabric layer). Rather than bundling all functionality into a single model endpoint, this architecture separates “thinking” from “coordination and execution.”
This separation becomes essential because agentic systems are inherently multi-step and heterogeneous. The traditional single-model-call does not scale when agents must query multiple models, interact with different tools, manage branching logic, and handle retries and failures.
Morgan Stanley Research

Morgan Stanley RESEARCH Idea So, as agentic usage grows, a dedicated fabric layer is required to manage model and tool routing, optimise for cost and latency, and ensure reliable execution. In this sense, agentic workflows directly create the need for this inference–fabric separation. • The Fabric layer includes: routing, memory, tool integration, policy enforcement, and observability functions. At the same time, separation improves agent capabilities. Once inference and fabric are decoupled, agentic systems become more scalable, controllable, and economically efficient. Amidst development of Agentic AI models, we are also seeing the maturing of chiplet-based designs spawned by the success of large AI/HPC designs. • A chiplet is a sort of pre-built 'block' of compute made to serve a function in a pre-optimised design. These blocks offer: • a logic subsystem (e.g. Arm's CSS chiplet), • a specialised accelerator (for running specific AI/ML workload tasks efficiently), • memory interface (e.g. off-load to High Bandwidth Memory, HBM), or • I/O (handle input/output operations, communication protocols and networking traffic).

AI Driven Emergence
Chiplet technology has transitioned from a niche approach to a mainstream design principle and is becoming the dominant methodology for high performance computing (HPC) and AI processors. And yet adoption is currently led by only a small group of tier one players in advanced segments.
One of the key advantages are the cost efficiencies. Chiplets enable the integration of mature process nodes for functions such as I/O alongside leading edge nodes for compute, mitigating rising costs at advanced nodes.
• Areas of Use. Leading chip companies (AMD, Apple, NVidia, Intel, etc.) have

adopted chiplet architectures for high end CPUs, GPUs, and server processors (e.g. AMD EPYC, Intel Ponte Vecchio, and Nvidia Blackwell). Other areas of use include ADAS systems in automotive and power efficient 3D-packaged designs in mobile.
• Drivers of Adoption. improved yields, cost efficiency, design flexibility (modularity, fast iteration, reuse)
Key challenges include design complexity (management of data flows and latency), packaging costs (interposers and 3D stacking), and thermal constraints (power density increases thermal management needs)(link).
Move Toward Standardisation
While early implementations were largely proprietary, we think 2025-26 marked a shift toward open standards aimed at broader ecosystem participation. Chiplet interface definitions remain early stage, but some are emerging. UCIe (universal chiplet interconnect express) is emerging as a critical standard, enabling interoperability across vendors. And work to standardise CXL (compute express link) for chiplets is actively occurring, primarily through the UCIe consortium, which adopted CXL as a key protocol for die-to-die communication.
We think other interface definitions in Boot ('I3C'), memory (for HBM/DRAM), EDA ('3Dblox'), low power ('bunch of wires' or BoW) and debug look set to follow. An adoption phase of these soon to be validated standards could follow (2026-28) as systems mature and applications grow. By 2029-30, the market could have achieved full maturity and widespread interoperability for complex multi-chiplet systems.
The notion of a proper, interoperable ‘chiplet marketplace’ may still be a little ways off, but it seems to be fast emerging as the industry delivers standards. Such a marketplace would help speed up deployment. And yet those with resources and key relationships, like Arm, are moving ahead faster than others.

As part of this, Arm have made available a new chiplet architecture to the open compute platform (OCP). Arm’s chiplet system architecture (CSA) has been worked on with partners for a while now (link). The idea is that this will abstract innovation up to the system level where it’s needed.
Arm and Meta first announced a chiplet-based partnership back in Oct'25 (link). Even then it was becoming clear that Meta would use Arm-based CPUs in data centers to power its AI ranking and recommendation systems. Described as a strategic, multi-year partnership, the collaboration involved Meta adopting Arm's technology for its critical AI workloads, providing validation for Arm based compute (Neoverse) following similar moves by other hyperscale cloud providers like AWS, Google, and Microsoft. The detail perhaps missed at the time was the work to port Meta's own ExecuTorch (software stack) to Arm. Meta's motivation, we think, stems from its heavy investment in AI and desire to optimize costs, improve efficiency within its AI infrastructure, and bring broader development to its OCP platform.
Bolt-on business acquisition targeted for Arm's high-speed interface know-how. Late last year, Arm announced plans to acquire DreamBig Semiconductor for development work in networking (Super NIC). Given DreamBig's chiplet product suite, such as the Deimos Chiplet Hub (link), we think the focus here in particular would be on new chiplet design development. With the proposed addition of this team, we think Arm would have enough to build its own chiplet design, potentially around DreamBig’s UCIe IP. It’s a small business with 100-200 engineers and seems likely to be a tuck-in that works alongside Arm's intent in developing deeper chiplet system know-how (link). The company has yet to close the deal - originally planned for March 2026 (c.$300m consideration).

The Rise of OpenClaw
We think the launch and record-breaking take-up of OpenClaw best exemplifies the impact of the emergence of Agentic AI.
OpenClaw is an open-source autonomous AI agent platform that functions as an operating system running locally on users’ devices. It can execute real-world tasks through persistent memory, tool execution, and deep integration with local environment and messaging apps.
• How it works? OpenClaw works by routing messages from messaging platforms through a central Gateway to an Agentic workload, which executes an agentic loop/workflow. As we outlined above, this assembles context from memory, invokes AI models to make decisions, executes tools, feeds results back to the model, and persists the updated state, creating a continuous reason-and-act cycle until the task is complete.

Deep Dive: The Arm AGI CPU
Agentic frameworks require power efficiency to deliver compute and inference; this is currently a bottleneck in AI frameworks. The 300W TDP and 3nm TSMC processor intends to target this constraint by maximising compute density to facilitate efficient power use. Below we highlight this and other specifics of Arm's new chip.
Design Principles. The new Arm AGI CPU chip is designed for agentic AI workloads in data centers. Specifically, it is for managing the orchestration, planning, and tool-use steps, rather than the raw, processing of data handled by GPUs. It has been built to match the needs of always-on AI agents, handling large orchestration tasks. Arm built the chip around three principles: performance, scale, and efficiency. Performance is critical, but the chip is also designed to efficiently scale to the rack and even data centre level.
Mid-market design. First glance gives you the impression that the AGI chip is solid but not loaded with ground-breaking specifications. Beyond a heavy core count and low power design, not much screams 'high end' in this CPU. The chip features 136 Arm cores (Neoverse V3) with a dedicated 2MB L2 cache and support for up to 3.7GHz speeds. The chip includes 96 lanes of PCIe Gen 6 with CXL 3 support, allowing connection to any accelerator and memory expansion capabilities. The memory system delivers up to 6GB/ s of DDR5 memory bandwidth to each core, with less than 100ns of latency, achieved through that dual-chiplet design where each chiplet has all memory and I/O directly on it. The chip operates at just 300W TDP (Thermal Design Power) and is built on a 3nm TSMC process. Put together, this is not a discount; it gives the chip broad market appeal whilst also enabling agentic workloads.
The chip also uses single-threading, which differs from the multi-threading designs of

Management have contrasted Arm's approach with legacy x86 architectures, stating that Arm is "focused on improving efficiency and reducing latency" rather than supporting legacy features. Arm emphasised that the chip is focused on what AGI data centers need; Arm aims to deliver full performance sustainably all the time without relying on unsustainable boost modes that increase power consumption, and achieves linear scaling across cores without the performance degradation seen with multi-threading approaches.

Key Metric: Performance per Watt
Arm claims its new CPU chip to be class-leading in performance-per-watt primarily by abandoning traditional, power-hungry features of x86 processors in favour of a specialised, high-density architecture optimised for agentic AI workloads. The chip, designed in collaboration with Meta, is intended to run AI inference tasks that are too general for GPUs but too intensive for legacy CPUs.
The claim to class-leading performance per watt is based on several architectural and design decisions:
• 136 Dedicated Neoverse V3 Cores: AGI features 136 Neoverse V3 cores. By using a "dedicated core per program thread," it eliminates the power overhead associated with Simultaneous Multi-threading (SMT) and reduces throttling under sustained load. It is this sustainability of CPU performance that Arm sees as an advantage in agentic workflows.
• High-Density, Lower-Power Infrastructure: The AGI CPU runs at a 300W TDP (Thermal Design Power), which means it generates up to 300 watts of heat under maximum theoretical load. At the same time, it is designed to fit into very dense configurations. This can be seen in the 45,000+ cores per liquid-cooled rack. This high density means less total infrastructure power is wasted on overhead compared to lower-density x86 systems.
Purpose-Built for Agentic AI: Unlike traditional CPUs designed for a wide range of tasks, this chip is specialised for agentic workflows (see above). This specialisation means the silicon is not wasting energy on unused, legacy functionality.
• Memory Bandwidth: The chip offers high-performance memory bandwidth (up to 800 GB/s using 12 channels of DDR5) designed to maintain high throughput in data-intensive AI agent scenarios.
• 2x Performance per Rack Advantage: Arm claims this architecture delivers over double the performance per rack compared to existing x86 platforms within the same power envelope. The chip is aimed at maximizing "usable compute" in data centers to keep operating costs low. However, these figures are based on Arm's own internal assessments, and independent validation is still needed.
